c: Oakridge Medical Group, a clinic with 40 employees moving into a new two-floor building
s: Oakridge Medical Group is moving into a new building in eight weeks. The clinic needs reliable wired and wireless access for exam-room computers, tablets, printers, an electronic health record system and guest Wi-Fi. The building has no existing network cabling. Patient data must be protected under privacy rules.

The office manager (judge) has a budget of $35,000 and wants a plan. The options are a wired network with a few access points, a mostly wireless design, or a hybrid with separate networks for staff and guests.
You have 7 minutes to explain your design, compare the alternatives with pros and cons, and recommend a plan.
f: Users: 40 staff, about 25 patient devices at a time
Floors: two, with 18 exam rooms and 6 offices
Fully wired design: about $29,000; mostly wireless: about $17,000; hybrid with VLANs: about $26,500
Privacy: medical records must be on a protected network, separate from guest Wi-Fi
Internet: a business fiber line with 500 Mbps
n: Identifies requirements: users, devices, bandwidth, reliability and privacy
Compares wired, wireless and hybrid designs with costs and pros and cons
Recommends a hybrid design with VLANs separating staff, medical and guest traffic
Describes equipment: switches, access points, firewall and cabling
Includes backups, redundancy and a timeline to be ready in eight weeks
Estimates cost against the $35,000 budget
q: Why can't guests use the same network as staff?
What happens if the main switch fails during clinic hours?
Can you finish in eight weeks?

c: Bluebird Accounting, a firm with 18 employees that handles client tax records
s: Bluebird Accounting discovered that an employee's laptop was infected with malware after clicking a link in a phishing email. The malware may have accessed a file server holding client tax records. The firm found out only because the antivirus alert popped up on one computer. There is no formal incident plan, and the firm's backups are stored on a drive that is always connected to the server.

The owner (judge) wants a plan to respond now and prevent future incidents. The budget is $12,000. Options include hiring an outside incident response firm, investing in endpoint protection and staff training, or setting up segmented networks with offline backups.
You have 7 minutes to present your analysis, compare the alternatives, and recommend a plan.
f: Employees: 18; clients: about 900 with sensitive tax and identity information
The infected laptop was disconnected 40 minutes after the alert
Backups: one external drive always attached to the server
Outside incident response: about $7,500; endpoint protection: $2,800 a year; training: $1,200; offline backup system: $2,000
Firms that handle tax data have legal duties to protect it and may have to notify clients
d: present your security response and prevention plan
n: Starts with containment and investigation steps: isolate, preserve evidence and check logs
Explains legal and client notification duties
Compares options with costs and pros and cons
Recommends a combination, such as incident response, offline backups and endpoint protection
Notes multi-factor authentication, patching and the principle of least privilege
Defines an incident response plan and ongoing training
q: Do we have to tell our clients?
Why is our backup drive a problem?
What is the first thing we should do in the next hour?

c: Cedar Hills High School, a school with 1,100 students and 90 staff
s: Teachers at Cedar Hills High School complain that the Wi-Fi slows to a crawl during class changes and testing. At the same time, students often connect to the school network on personal phones and games, and some students have gotten into restricted areas. The network team has one full-time administrator and a small budget.
The principal (judge) wants you to explain what is causing the problems and what can be done within a $15,000 budget before state testing in six weeks.
You have 7 minutes to present your analysis, compare the alternatives and recommend a plan.
f: Access points: 28, many over seven years old
Peak demand: about 2,000 devices at once
Internet bandwidth: 300 Mbps shared by the whole school
New access points: $450 each; bandwidth upgrade to 1 Gbps: $350 a month extra
Content filtering and access control upgrade: $3,200
n: Diagnoses likely causes: aging access points, limited bandwidth and too many unmanaged devices
Compares upgrading access points, adding bandwidth and enforcing policies
Recommends a priority order that fits $15,000 (about 12 new access points in the busiest areas, access control and a bandwidth upgrade)
Explains monitoring tools and how to set quality of service for testing
Covers user accounts, permissions and acceptable use
Describes how to measure improvement
q: Which classrooms do you fix first?
How do you protect state testing from interruptions?
How would you manage student devices without blocking learning?

c: Willow Street Cafe, a cafe adding a second location
s: Willow Street Cafe is opening a second location in five weeks and needs a network for point-of-sale terminals, a kitchen display, security cameras, music streaming and customer Wi-Fi. The owner has no IT staff and wants the setup to be reliable and secure. The owner is deciding between a managed service plan, buying equipment and installing it with a contractor, or using a consumer router setup.
The owner (judge) has $6,500 for the network. You must explain what equipment is needed, how it should be configured, and which option to choose.
You have 7 minutes to present your plan, compare the alternatives, and recommend a setup.
f: Devices: 3 point-of-sale terminals, 1 kitchen display, 4 cameras, 1 music player, guest Wi-Fi for about 30 customers
Managed service: $5,800 for equipment plus $90 a month
Contractor-installed business equipment: $4,900 once
Consumer router setup: $350, no separation of networks
Payment card rules require the payment network to be separate from guest Wi-Fi
n: Lists the equipment: router or firewall, switch, access point, cabling
Explains configuring separate networks (VLANs or guest isolation) and why payment systems must be separated
Compares managed service, contractor install and consumer gear with pros and cons
Explains IP addressing, DHCP and password management at a basic level
Recommends the contractor-installed or managed option and defends the cost
Describes testing and documentation before opening
q: Why can't I just use a regular home router?
What happens if the internet goes down in the middle of lunch?
Who changes the passwords when an employee leaves?

c: Harbor Logistics, a shipping company with a warehouse and 3 satellite offices
s: Harbor Logistics's employees at three small offices connect to the warehouse's systems over slow, unreliable links, and remote staff often use shared passwords to access files. Some video calls and the inventory application stall during busy periods. The IT director wants a secure, reliable way for remote offices and traveling staff to reach company systems.
The IT director (judge) has a budget of $20,000. The options are site-to-site VPNs with business internet, a cloud-based remote access service, or upgrading all sites to dedicated private lines.
You have 7 minutes to explain the protocols and services involved, compare the alternatives with pros and cons, and recommend a plan.
f: Satellite offices: 3 with 6 to 12 staff each; 25 remote staff
Current setup: shared accounts and unencrypted connections to some systems
Site-to-site VPN with business-class internet: about $9,000 plus $350 a month
Cloud remote access service: about $12 per user per month
Dedicated private lines: about $1,600 a month per site
n: Explains VPNs, encryption and authentication in plain language
Compares site-to-site VPNs, a cloud access service and private lines on cost, performance and security
Calculates annual costs of each option
Recommends unique user accounts and multi-factor authentication
Considers quality of service for video and the inventory application
Provides a rollout plan with a pilot at one office
q: Why is a shared password such a problem?
Would a VPN be fast enough for the inventory system?
How would you handle someone who loses a laptop?
